title: The Quest for Reliable Metrics of Responsible AI
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to evaluate responsible AI systems reliably, with a particular focus on fairness metrics used in recommender systems. The authors argue that although many metrics exist, their robustness, interpretability, and mathematical validity are often insufficiently examined, which can make metric scores misleading or unstable.

Rather than studying a classroom, school, or K-12 intervention, the paper synthesizes prior work on fairness evaluation in recommender systems and extends those lessons to AI in science (AIS). The approach is conceptual and reflective: the authors review prior analyses of metric limitations, describe issues such as invalid mathematical operations, unknown or unreachable score ranges, low sensitivity, and redundancy, and then propose corrected metrics and new evaluation approaches.

The paper offers practical guidelines for designing reliable metrics of responsible AI, including questions to ask about validity, range, sensitivity, and redundancy. Its main conclusion is that metric development itself must be treated as a core part of responsible AI, because evaluation scores can be unreliable or overstate fairness if metric limitations are ignored. The guidelines are intended to generalize beyond recommender systems to AIS and other AI applications.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/reflection paper and guidelines piece, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It does not present a controlled design, participant data, or causal evaluation relevant to K-12 efficacy criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has indirect impact by improving how AI systems may be evaluated and governed, but it does not measure learner outcomes. Its relevance is mainly conceptual and methodological, so any practical impact is unclear and modest.

interventions.use_case: Methodological analysis of fairness and responsible-AI evaluation metrics for AI systems, with examples drawn from recommender systems and broader AI-in-science contexts rather than a student-facing educational tool.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that reliable evaluation metrics are necessary for responsible AI governance and policy, especially in high-stakes AI-in-science contexts. It does not report an experimental effect size; instead, it provides guidelines and conceptual evidence that flawed metrics can mislead policy and evaluation practice.
finding.measure: Robustness/reliability of fairness evaluation metrics; interpretability and validity of metric scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes corrected metrics and new evaluation approaches that are intended to make responsible-AI assessment easier and more usable in practice. It reports that some existing metrics can crash, have unreachable ranges, or be redundant, implying that better metric design can improve the efficiency and reliability of evaluation workflows.
finding.measure: Metric computability, score-range interpretability, sensitivity, redundancy
